pradeep|Chemistry|0|14|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Two steps, and neither of them is an oxidation.
**Step 1 — NBS in light.** N-Bromosuccinimide with hv is the reagent for **allylic
bromination**. It supplies bromine at a very low concentration, which suppresses addition
across the double bond and allows free-radical substitution at the **allylic** C–H instead.
The double bond therefore **survives**:
4,4-dimethylcyclohexene ⟶ 3-bromo-5,5-dimethylcyclohexene
**Step 2 — H₂O with K₂CO₃.** Mild aqueous base hydrolyses the allylic bromide. The allylic
cation is stabilised by resonance, so this goes readily by SN1, and water supplies the
hydroxyl:
⟶ the **allylic alcohol**, with the C=C still in place ✓ — option (b)
So the product X is the unsaturated alcohol.
The distractors each correspond to a reaction that did not happen:
**(c)** the **ketone** would require an oxidation of the alcohol, and neither NBS/hv nor
K₂CO₃/H₂O oxidises
**(d)** the **carboxylic acid** would require a still stronger oxidation
**(a)** the unchanged alkene would mean no reaction at all
The point of the question is to recognise **NBS/hv** as the allylic substitution reagent. Had
the reagent been Br₂ in CCl₄ in the dark, the bromine would have **added** across the double
bond instead, and the answer would be quite different.
∴ option (b).

Note: the printed key gives (c), the ketone. Neither step in the sequence is an oxidation,
so the product is the allylic alcohol; the key is wrong and has been corrected to (b).

pradeep|Chemistry|0|22|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Nucleophilicity of the halide ions depends on the **solvent**, and the two cases give
opposite orders. The convention, unless an aprotic solvent is named, is the **protic**
(aqueous or alcoholic) one.
**In a protic solvent** — water, methanol, ethanol:
**I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > F⁻**
so in **increasing** order, **Cl⁻ < Br⁻ < I⁻** ✓ — option (c)
The reason is **solvation**. A protic solvent hydrogen-bonds to the anion, and the smaller
the anion the more tightly it is held. **F⁻ and Cl⁻ are small and densely charged**, so they
are wrapped in a thick solvent shell that must be stripped away before they can attack.
**I⁻ is large and polarisable**, holds its solvent loosely, and is therefore the most
effective nucleophile despite being the **weakest base**.
**In a polar aprotic solvent** — DMF, DMSO, acetone — there is no hydrogen bonding to the
anion, the ions are 'naked', and nucleophilicity then follows **basicity**:
**F⁻ > Cl⁻ > Br⁻ > I⁻**, so increasing would be I⁻ < Br⁻ < Cl⁻
That is the order the printed key assumes, but the question names no aprotic solvent.
The lesson is that nucleophilicity is not an intrinsic property of an ion — it depends on
what the ion is dissolved in, and the halides are the standard illustration.
∴ Cl⁻ < Br⁻ < I⁻.

Note: the printed key gives (b), which is the order in a **polar aprotic** solvent. No such
solvent is specified, and the conventional (protic) order is the reverse, so the key has
been corrected to (c).

pradeep|Chemistry|0|23|Pradeep Chemistry:
Test the four statements against the mechanism drawn, which is the stepwise **SN1** route
through an ion pair.
**(i) Favoured by weak nucleophiles** ✓ **correct.** The slow step is the **ionisation** of
R–X; the nucleophile takes no part in it, so the rate does not depend on the nucleophile at
all. A weak nucleophile simply means SN2 cannot compete, leaving SN1 the dominant path.
**(ii) R⁺ formed easily if the substituents are bulky** ✓ **correct**, for two reasons. Bulky
alkyl groups are usually **more substituted**, so they stabilise the cation by induction and
hyperconjugation; and the crowded sp³ carbon becomes a **planar** sp² cation, which
**relieves steric strain**.
**(iii) Accompanied by racemization** ✓ **correct.** The carbocation is **planar**, so the
nucleophile can attack either face with roughly equal probability, giving both enantiomers.
**(iv) Favoured by non-polar solvents** ✗ **wrong.** The slow step creates a pair of **ions**
from a neutral molecule, so it needs a **polar** solvent to stabilise the developing charges.
A polar **protic** solvent is best of all, since it can hydrogen-bond to the leaving halide.
So (i), (ii) and (iii) are correct ✓ — option (c).
The single statement that fails is the one about solvent, and it fails for the clearest
reason of all: making ions in a non-polar medium is energetically hopeless.
∴ (i), (ii) and (iii).
pradeep|Chemistry|0|24|Pradeep Chemistry:
SN1 requires the halide to ionise to a **carbocation**, and a carbocation must be **planar**,
with the empty p orbital perpendicular to the three remaining bonds.
**(c) the bridgehead halide** ✓ **inactive.** The chlorine sits at the **bridgehead** of a
bicyclic cage. A carbocation there would have to become planar, but the rigid ring system
physically **cannot flatten** at that carbon — the bridges hold it pyramidal. The cation
cannot form, so SN1 is impossible ✓
(SN2 is impossible too, for a different reason: the backside of the C–Cl bond is buried
inside the cage, so no nucleophile can approach from behind. Bridgehead halides are
notoriously unreactive by **both** mechanisms.)
The others all ionise readily:
**(a) (CH₃)₃CCl** — tert-butyl chloride, giving a stable planar **tertiary** cation
**(b) an allylic chloride** — giving a resonance-stabilised **allyl** cation
**(d) C₆H₅CHClCH₃** — giving a resonance-stabilised **benzylic** cation
This is an instance of **Bredt's rule**, which forbids a double bond (and by extension a
planar sp² centre) at the bridgehead of a small bicyclic system. The same rule explains why
bridgehead halides will not eliminate either.
∴ option (c).
pradeep|Chemistry|0|25|Pradeep Chemistry:
**Complete inversion** means the reaction goes **purely by SN2**, with no SN1 competing — for
any SN1 character would bring racemisation with it. So the compound must undergo clean,
exclusive backside attack.
Take the four:
**(c) (CH₃)₃CCl** ✗ — **tertiary**. The carbon is too crowded for backside attack, and the
cation is so stable that the reaction goes entirely by **SN1**, with racemisation. No
inversion at all.
**(a) CH₃Cl** ✗ — it does undergo SN2 faster than any of the others, but the carbon carries
**three identical hydrogens**. There is no configuration to invert, so 'complete
stereochemical inversion' cannot be spoken of.
**(b) (C₂H₅)₂CHCl** ✗ — secondary, but with **two ethyl groups** flanking the reaction centre
it is appreciably hindered, so SN2 is slow and SN1 can compete.
**(d) (CH₃)₂CHCl** ✓ — secondary, with the **two smallest possible** alkyl groups. It is the
least hindered of the secondary halides offered, so backside attack is easy and the reaction
proceeds cleanly by SN2 with **complete inversion** of configuration at the carbon.
The underlying principle is the reactivity order for SN2:
**methyl > primary > secondary ≫ tertiary**
and the fact that SN2 always inverts, because the nucleophile must attack from the side
opposite the leaving group — the umbrella turning inside out.
∴ (CH₃)₂CHCl.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|28|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
SN2 is a **backside attack**: the nucleophile must reach the carbon from the side opposite
the leaving group, through the transition state in which five groups crowd around one
carbon. The rate is therefore governed almost entirely by **steric hindrance**, and the
least crowded halide reacts fastest.
All four here are **primary** bromides, so the decisive factor is **branching at the β
carbon** — the carbon next to the one being attacked.
**(b) CH₃CH₂Br** ✓ **fastest.** Only a methyl group beyond the reaction centre; essentially
nothing in the way.
**(c) CH₃CH₂CH₂Br** — an ethyl group beyond; slightly slower.
**(d) (CH₃)₂CHCH₂Br** — isobutyl bromide, with **one branch** at the β carbon. Noticeably
slower.
**(a) (CH₃)₃CCH₂Br** ✗ **slowest by far.** This is **neopentyl bromide**. Although the carbon
bearing the bromine is primary, the **tert-butyl group right beside it** blocks the backside
approach completely. Neopentyl halides are about 10⁵ times slower than ethyl in SN2 — famous
for being primary halides that will not do SN2.
So the order is **ethyl > n-propyl > isobutyl ≫ neopentyl**, and ethyl bromide is the
fastest.
The lesson is that 'primary' is not by itself a guarantee of SN2 reactivity: what matters is
the room around the carbon, including the **β** substituents.
∴ CH₃CH₂Br.

Note: the printed key gives (d), isobutyl bromide, which is branched at the β carbon and
therefore slower than the unbranched ethyl bromide; the key is wrong and has been corrected
to (b).

pradeep|Chemistry|0|29|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
The reaction is an **SN2** substitution by an **anionic** nucleophile, CN⁻, and for that the
best solvent is a **polar aprotic** one.
**(c) DMF, N,N-dimethylformamide** ✓ — polar enough to dissolve the ionic NaCN, but with
**no O–H or N–H** to hydrogen-bond to the anion. The sodium ion is solvated by the carbonyl
oxygen while the **cyanide is left essentially bare**, free to attack at full strength. SN2
rates in DMF or DMSO are often a **thousand times** faster than in water or an alcohol.
The others are **polar protic** solvents and all slow the reaction down:
**(a) ethanol**, **(b) methanol**, **(d) water**
Each has an O–H that hydrogen-bonds to CN⁻, surrounding it in a cage of solvent molecules.
Before the cyanide can attack, that cage must be stripped away, and the energy needed to do
so raises the activation barrier.
So the rule for SN2 with an anionic nucleophile is: **use a polar aprotic solvent** — DMF,
DMSO, acetone or acetonitrile.
The contrast with **SN1** is instructive and often examined. SN1 needs exactly the opposite:
a polar **protic** solvent, because its slow step creates ions and the hydrogen bonding that
hampers SN2 is precisely what stabilises the departing halide and speeds SN1 up.
∴ N,N′-dimethylformamide (DMF).

Note: the printed key gives (b), methanol, a protic solvent that solvates the cyanide and
slows the reaction; the key is wrong and has been corrected to (c).

pradeep|Chemistry|0|31|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
An SN1 reaction at a chiral centre goes through a **planar carbocation**, which can in
principle be attacked from either face with equal probability. Complete racemisation would
follow — but in practice it is never quite complete.
What actually happens is **partial racemisation with a small excess of inversion** ✓ —
option (a).
The reason is the **ion pair**. When the leaving group departs it does not instantly diffuse
away; for a brief moment it lingers on the face it left from, **shielding that side** of the
cation. The nucleophile therefore finds the opposite face slightly more accessible, and a
little more inverted product is formed than retained.
Typical results are **5–20 % net inversion** on top of the racemic mixture, the exact figure
depending on how quickly the ion pair separates — which in turn depends on the solvent and
on how stable the cation is. A very stable, long-lived cation comes closer to full
racemisation; a short-lived one shows more inversion.
Why the other options are wrong:
**(d) 100 % racemization** ✗ would be true only if the free cation were completely symmetrical
in its surroundings, which the ion pair prevents.
**(b) 100 % retention** ✗ is the opposite of what the ion pair produces.
**(c) 100 % conversion** ✗ is a statement about **yield**, not stereochemistry, so it does not
answer the question at all.
The contrast is with **SN2**, which gives **100 % inversion** every time, because there is no
intermediate for the leaving group to shield.
∴ inversion more than retention leading to partial racemization.

Note: the printed key gives (c), '100 % conversion', which is not a stereochemical outcome.
The key is wrong and has been corrected to (a).

pradeep|Chemistry|0|34|Pradeep Chemistry:
2-Chloro-2-methylpentane is a **tertiary** halide, and sodium methoxide in methanol supplies
both a **strong nucleophile** and a **strong base**. Both substitution and elimination occur,
so all three products are formed ✓ — option (a).
**(I) The ether**, C₂H₅CH₂C(CH₃)₂–OCH₃ — the **substitution** product. A tertiary halide
cannot do SN2, but in methanol it ionises readily to the tertiary carbocation, which
methoxide (or methanol) captures by **SN1**.
**(II) and (III) The two alkenes** — the **elimination** products. Methoxide removes a
β-hydrogen, and there are **two different kinds** of β-hydrogen available:
from the **methyl** group ⟹ C₂H₅CH₂C(CH₃)=CH₂, the less substituted **Hofmann** product (II)
from the **CH₂** of the chain ⟹ C₂H₅CH=C(CH₃)CH₃, the more substituted **Zaitsev** product
(III), which predominates among the alkenes
So the flask contains all three, and the answer is 'all of these'.
The general rule the question illustrates: a **tertiary halide with a strong base** gives
mainly elimination, but substitution is never absent, and where more than one β-hydrogen is
available, more than one alkene forms. Only a **bulky** base such as tert-butoxide would
push the product almost entirely towards the Hofmann alkene.
∴ all of these.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|46|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
**Enantiomeric excess** measures how far a mixture departs from being racemic. It is defined
as the **difference** between the percentages of the two enantiomers:
**ee = |% of one enantiomer − % of the other|**
Substituting:
ee = 85 − 15 = **70 %** ✓ — option (c)
The sense of the definition is worth seeing. Of the 85 % and 15 %, the 15 % of each pairs off
into a **30 % racemic** mixture, which is optically inactive. What is left over is
85 − 15 = **70 %** of pure single enantiomer, and only that part contributes any rotation.
So the mixture behaves as 70 % pure enantiomer plus 30 % racemate.
That is also why ee has a direct experimental meaning:
**observed rotation = ee × rotation of the pure enantiomer**
so a mixture with 70 % ee shows 70 % of the specific rotation of the pure compound. Measuring
the rotation is in fact how ee is usually determined, and the quantity is sometimes called
the **optical purity** for that reason.
The limits are worth noting: ee = 0 for a **racemic** mixture (50:50) and ee = 100 % for a
single pure enantiomer.
Option (a), 85 %, is the commonest error — quoting the proportion of the major enantiomer
instead of the excess.
∴ 70 %.

Note: the printed key gives (a), 85 %, which is the amount of the major enantiomer, not the
excess. Enantiomeric excess is 85 − 15 = 70 %, so the key is wrong and has been corrected
to (c).

pradeep|Chemistry|0|51|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
**Retention** of configuration happens when the chiral centre is **not involved** in the
reaction at all — the nucleophile attacks somewhere else and leaves the stereocentre
untouched.
So look for the compound whose **halogen is on a carbon that is not the chiral one**.
**(d) CH₃–CH(C₆H₅)–CH₂Br** ✓
The **chiral centre** is the carbon bearing CH₃, C₆H₅, H and CH₂Br — four different groups.
But the **bromine is on the terminal CH₂**, a **primary** carbon carrying two hydrogens,
which is **not** a stereocentre. OH⁻ attacks there by SN2; the chiral carbon is never
touched, so its configuration is **retained** ✓
The others all have the halogen **on** the chiral carbon, so attack there inverts it:
**(a) CH₃–CHBr–C₆H₁₃** — chiral (CH₃, H, Br, hexyl), SN2 ⟹ **inversion**
**(b) CH₃–CHBr–C₆H₅** — chiral and benzylic, so SN1 competes ⟹ **racemisation**
**(c) CH₃–CHBr–CH₃** — isopropyl bromide, with **two identical methyls**, so it is **not
chiral** at all and the question of retention does not arise
The principle to carry away: in a nucleophilic substitution, the stereochemical outcome is
decided entirely by **where the attack occurs**. SN2 at a stereocentre always inverts, SN1 at
a stereocentre racemises, and attack anywhere else leaves the molecule's configuration
unchanged.
∴ CH₃–CH(C₆H₅)–CH₂Br.

Note: the printed key gives (a), where the bromine sits on the chiral carbon itself and SN2
would invert it. The key is wrong and has been corrected to (d). The book's own explanation
on a later page confirms it: 'Compound (d) contains a chiral centre but the reaction occurs
on a carbon which is not chiral, therefore retention of configuration occurs.'

pradeep|Chemistry|0|53|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
The three reagents form a sequence, and each step tests something.
**(i) NaOH** hydrolyses the halide, releasing the halide ion into solution — **but only if the
halogen is attached to an sp³ carbon**. An **aryl** halide does not hydrolyse: its C–X bond
has partial double-bond character from resonance with the ring, and there is no site for
backside attack.
**(ii) dil. HNO₃** neutralises the excess alkali, so that the silver is not precipitated as
Ag₂O.
**(iii) AgNO₃** then precipitates whatever halide was released, and the **colour identifies
it**: AgCl **white**, AgBr **pale yellow**, AgI **yellow**.
Now the four compounds:
**I, II** — aryl **chlorides**. No hydrolysis, so **no precipitate** at all ✗
**III** — an aryl **bromide**. Again no hydrolysis ✗
**IV** ✓ — it carries an aryl Cl **and** a **–CH₂I** group. The benzylic iodide is on an sp³
carbon and hydrolyses readily, releasing **I⁻**, which gives the **yellow** precipitate of
**AgI** ✓ (The aryl chlorine stays put and contributes nothing.)
So only compound IV responds — option (d).
Two things had to be right: the halogen must be on a **saturated** carbon to be released at
all, and it must be **iodide** for the precipitate to be yellow rather than white.
∴ compound IV.

Note: the printed key gives (b), an aryl chloride, which neither hydrolyses nor could give a
yellow precipitate. The key is wrong and has been corrected to (d).
